title: Gadadhara Dasa
html:
Gadadhara of the Dasa Family

Listing the branches of Sri Chaitanya's tree, Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks of him briefly and solemnly:

“Sri Gadadhara Dasa is a branch above all others; he made even the Kazis utter the name of Hari.” (CC, Adi 10.53)

Vrindavana Dasa Thakura calls him Gadadhara Dasa and Gadadhara Mahashaya, and says that he “was infinitely dear to the Lord” and that “his body was filled with the sweetness of loving service” (CB, Antya 5.93). Kavi Karnapura in the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” calls him “Gadadhara of the Dasa family” (dasa-vamsha-gadadhara), and later generations call him Dasa Gadadhara, Sri Gadadhara Dasa Thakura, Srila Gadadhara Dasa Prabhu. He should not be confused with Gadadhara Pandita, the Lord's eternal companion and shakti.1

Of his worldly life the sources say almost nothing. They name neither his parents nor the year or day of his appearance; Karnapura tells us only that he was of the Dasa family. Nor is the day of his appearance found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

His shripat is Ariadaha (Eriyadaha, Endiyadaha) on the bank of the Bhagirathi; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.53 places it four kroshas north of Calcutta. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” calls him “Gadadhara Dasa of Endiyadaha,” and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” speaks of the Kazi who lived “in this village of Endiyadaha.”2

The Radiance of Radha

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“Chandrakanti, who was a manifestation of Radha's glory, is now near Gauranga as Gadadhara of the Dasa family.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 154)

And he adds at once:

“Purnananda, who in Vraja was foremost among the beloveds of Baladeva, also entered into this Gadadhara for the sake of the work.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 155)

Thus two were united in Gadadhara Dasa: Chandrakanti, the radiance of Radha, and Purnananda, the beloved companion of Balarama; one of the biographies calls him plainly their union. This entering is not possession in any worldly sense but the spiritual presence (avesha) of Baladeva's eternal companion, who came to serve Nityananda, Baladeva Himself; and so Gadadhara Dasa, though his whole heart belonged to madhura-rasa, remained at Nityananda's side all his life.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, in his “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.53, explains the difference between the two Gadadharas. Gadadhara Pandita is the very form of the daughter of Vrishabhanu, while Gadadhara Dasa is the beauty of Her body (anga-shobha), Her radiance (kanti). Gaura is Krishna endowed with the mood and radiance of Radha (radha-bhava-dyuti-suvalita), and Gadadhara Dasa is that radiance (dyuti) of Gaura.3

Therefore he is counted among the associates of both Gaura and Nityananda. The “Charitamrita” says:

“Sri Ramadasa and Gadadhara Dasa, devotees of Chaitanya Gosani, stayed at Nityananda's side. When Mahaprabhu told Nityananda to go to Gauda, He sent these two with Him. Therefore they are counted in both groups, and so it is with Madhava and Vasudeva Ghosha.” (CC, Adi 11.13–15)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains: the followers of Gaura are connoisseurs of the madhura-rasa of Vraja, while the followers of Nityananda serve in sakhya and the other rasas where pure devotion is foremost. Gadadhara Dasa, though he belonged to Nityananda's circle, is not a cowherd boy in the mood of friendship but a connoisseur of madhura-rasa. In the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls him “an eternally perfect resident of Vraja” (nitya-siddha vraja-jana), in whom the transcendental (aprakrita) bhava of Radha is manifest.

With Mahaprabhu in Navadvipa

Before the Lord sent him with Nityananda to Gauda, Gadadhara Dasa lived with Mahaprabhu Himself; that is why the “Charitamrita” calls him and Ramadasa “devotees of Sri Chaitanya” (Adi 11.13).

Of the days in Navadvipa sing the padas of his disciple Yadunandana and of Narahari (apparently Chakravarti), preserved in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12) and the “Gaura-pada-tarangini.” Gaura, weeping “Radha!”, embraces Gadai, while Dasa Gadadhara softly smiles; Gaura exchanges glances with him, holds his hand in kirtana, weeps on his lap. “Gaura is the life of Dasa Gadadhara,” sings the poet, and Gadadhara Dasa shines beside Gaura “like a moon beside the moon.” Another pada of Narahari sings of Nityananda going to Gadadhara Dasa's house, calling “Gora!”, like an elephant intoxicated with prema.

Lochana Dasa in the “Chaitanya-mangala” names him among those who danced in Advaita's house at Shantipur when the Lord came there after His sannyasa.4 In Karnapura's drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” (act 10) he is among the Gaudiya devotees going to the Lord in Puri whom Sarvabhauma meets.

The “Charitamrita” also tells how in Puri the non-brahmanas — Vasudeva Datta, Gadadhara, Murari Gupta, and the residents of Kulinagrama and Khanda — invited the Lord and fed Him with Jagannatha's prasada bought in the market (Antya 10.140–141). Whether this is the same Gadadhara is hard to say.5

With Nityananda to Gauda

When Mahaprabhu resolved to open the treasure of divine love to Gauda, He sent Nityananda there:

“To Nityananda He gave this order: ‘Go to Gauda and reveal loving devotion freely, without restraint. I am sending Ramadasa, Gadadhara and a few others along to help You. From time to time I will come to You, and, staying unseen, I will watch You dance.’” (CC, Madhya 15.42–44)

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” explains that this Gadadhara is Gadadhara Dasa. Vrindavana Dasa lists all who set out from Puri with Nityananda:

“With Nityananda went Ramadasa, Gadadhara Dasa, Raghunatha Vaidya, full of the sweetness of loving devotion, Krishnadasa Pandita, Parameshvari Dasa and the jubilant Purandara Pandita.” (CB, Antya 5.231–233)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that this was in the Shaka year 1434 (about 1512–1513) and that Gadadhara Dasa became one of Nityananda's chief helpers in the preaching: he taught everyone to repeat the name of Hari.6

Already on the way Nityananda's companions, overwhelmed by love, forgot the outer world, and in each his eternal mood became manifest. Ramadasa stood bent in three places like a cowherd boy, and Gadadhara Dasa —

“Gadadhara Dasa was filled with the mood of Radhika. Laughing loudly, he cried, ‘Who will buy yogurt?’” (CB, Antya 5.238)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya”: in Radha's bhava, like a girl of Vraja selling yogurt, he forgot his outward identity, and Nityananda saw this.7

“Who Will Buy Milk?”

Having come to Gauda, Nityananda toured the villages on either bank of the Ganga, and one day He came to the house of Gadadhara Dasa:

“One day Nityananda came to the house of Gadadhara Dasa to show him His affection. The great soul Gadadhara Dasa was absorbed in the mood of a gopi and full of the highest bliss. Carrying a pot of Ganga water on his head, he called out without cease, ‘Who will buy milk?’” (CB, Antya 5.371–373)

In his temple sat a beautiful Bala-Gopala whom he served. Seeing his host's bhava, Nityananda took up Bala-Gopala, pressed Him to His chest, roared like a lion and began to dance in the mood of a cowherd boy, while all around loudly sang the names of the Lord (CB, Antya 5.374–377).8

Then Madhavananda Ghosha, the brother of Vasudeva Ghosha, sang of the dana-lila, and a wonderful bhava arose in Nityananda; His dancing was beyond description (CB, Antya 5.378–383). The Dana-keli is a pastime of Krishna with the gopis: Krishna and His friends bar the way of the girls carrying milk products to market and demand a “toll” from them; Srila Rupa Gosvami described it in the “Dana-keli-kaumudi.” This lila Nityananda revealed in Gadadhara's house through kirtana and dance, and since then his temple has been renowned as the site of the dana-lila. The “Charitamrita” says:

“Gadadhara Dasa was full of bliss in the mood of a gopi, and in his house Nityananda revealed the dana-keli pastime. Sri Madhava Ghosha was foremost among the kirtana singers, and Nityananda Prabhu would dance to his singing.” (CC, Adi 11.17–18)9

Nityananda stayed in his house for several days, hearing the dana-khanda from Madhavananda and bestowing mercy on many. And Gadadhara Dasa himself was unaware of the outer world:

“In the mood of a gopi Gadadhara Dasa had no outward awareness; at every moment he thought of himself as a gopi.” (CB, Antya 5.381)

Unconscious of his body, he kept urging everyone: “Haribol! Haribol!” (CB, Antya 5.393–394).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on this verse explains: Gadadhara Dasa always abided in his eternal spiritual form (svarupa-siddhi), and yet he never outwardly assumed a sakhi's dress; ever absorbed in the bhava of a gopi, he displayed no pretence in dress. His gopi mood is not worldly femininity and not imitation but his eternal nature, the radiance of Radha; therefore he had no need of anything outward. Failing to understand his divine madness of love, wilful people later invented the community of “sakhi-bhekis”: conscious of themselves as men, they dress the body in women's clothes. No acharya following Srila Rupa Gosvami ever approved this path; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls it a degradation, an obstacle to devotion (“Gaudiya-bhashya” on CB, Antya 5.238).

Murari Gupta relates (4.22.13–15) that when Nityananda came to the house of Gadadhara, who was full of the gopi bhava, Gadadhara, seeing Him, was overwhelmed with love and went with Him in kirtana to Saptagrama; there, on the bank of the Triveni, while the qualities of Gauranga were sung, he danced in the highest bliss, revealing the mood of a gopi.

The Kazi of Ariadaha

In Ariadaha lived a powerful Kazi, the ruler of the village, an enemy of religion who hated kirtana. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta adds in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” that whoever failed to show him respect he deprived of caste; people feared him and fled from him.

One night Gadadhara Dasa, intoxicated with love of God, went straight to his house. Vrindavana Dasa tells:

“The people, in fear of that Kazi, would flee from him; but Gadadhara fearlessly went to his house at night. Ceaselessly calling the name of Hari, he entered the Kazi's house. The Kazi's men saw him, and not one of them could utter a word.” (CB, Antya 5.397–399)

Ceaselessly calling out the name of Hari, he summoned the master:

“Gadadhara said: ‘Hey, where is that Kazi? Say “Krishna” at once, or I will cut off your head!’” (CB, Antya 5.400)

This is not a threat of violence but the speech of one intoxicated with prema — so Nityananda too spoke to the godless, and so the Lord Himself came with kirtana to Chand Kazi. And it was not force that softened the Kazi, but the form and bhava of the devotee.

“The Kazi came out blazing with anger like fire, but the moment he saw Gadadhara Dasa he grew still.” (CB, Antya 5.401)

His anger subsided, his face turned friendly, and he asked: “Gadadhara, why are you here?” Gadadhara answered that he had come to say something important:

“Sri Chaitanya and Nityananda Prabhu have descended and made the whole world say ‘Hari, Hari.’ You alone do not say the name of Hari; I have come to you to make you say it. Say the name of Hari, the supreme blessing, and I will deliver you from all your sins.” (CB, Antya 5.403–405)

Cruel by nature though he was, the Kazi stood stunned and could not say a word. Then he smiled and said: “Listen, Dasa Gadadhara. I will say ‘Hari’ tomorrow; today go home” (CB, Antya 5.406–407).10

But the Name had already sounded from his lips, and Gadadhara Dasa was filled with the happiness of love:

“Gadadhara Dasa said: ‘Why tomorrow? You have just said “Hari” yourself, with your own mouth! Since you have taken the name of Hari, there is no more misfortune for you, not for a moment.’” (CB, Antya 5.409–410)

With these words, in the highest ecstasy of love, he began to dance, clapping his hands (CB, Antya 5.411). The same reply — “Why tomorrow? You have just uttered ‘Hari’ with your own mouth” — Srila Bhaktisiddhanta also cites in his “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.53.

Thus the dreaded Kazi, from whom the whole countryside fled, received the name of Hari. Whence did Gadadhara have such power? Vrindavana Dasa answers:

“After a while Gadadhara returned to his own house — he in whose body Nityananda abides.” (CB, Antya 5.412)

Gadadhara's body was the abode of Nityananda: what acted in him was Nityananda's power, not the personal power of a man. One of the biographies says that he delivered the Kazi “by his transcendental power,” another that “Krishna abided in his body”; the sense is one: only one whom Krishna has empowered can spread the name of Hari. Vallabha Bhatta says this to the Lord:

“The dharma of the age of Kali is the sankirtana of Krishna's name. Without Krishna's power no one can propagate it.” (CC, Antya 7.11)

And further: “Without Krishna's power prema is not manifested” (CC, Antya 7.14).11

Saintly people would not even come near this Kazi for fear of losing caste, yet Gadadhara Dasa bestowed on him a merciful glance; and that a cruel man gave up his cruelty Vrindavana Dasa calls the work of Krishna within His devotee (CB, Antya 5.414–416). As Gaurasundara Himself in Mayapur came at the head of the sankirtana to Chand Kazi and made him utter the Name, so His servant Gadadhara Dasa made the Kazi of his own village utter the name of Hari: the servant follows in the footsteps of the Lord.

But is it not an offence to give the Name to the faithless? Every sattvata scripture, and Srila Jiva Gosvami as well, counts instructing the faithless in the Name among the offences against the Name. One of the biographies answers: Gadadhara Dasa did not encourage this offence. He is the very merciful shakti of Gaura-Nityananda, and he endowed even the hostile Kazi with a special power of mercy, as Narada once showed mercy to Nalakuvara and Manigriva. The prohibition of the scriptures remains in force; here is the special mercy of a great soul — and the Kazi, moreover, had already uttered the name of Hari himself.

The Lord's Mercy at Panihati

When Mahaprabhu, wishing to go to Vrindavana, set out through Gauda, He met the devotees at Shantipur and Kumarahatta and came to Panihati, to the house of Raghava Pandita. Hearing of this, Gadadhara Dasa hurried there:

“As soon as Gadadhara Dasa heard that Sri Gaurasundara was in Raghava's house, he hurried there at once. Gadadhara Dasa was infinitely dear to the Lord; his body was filled with the sweetness of loving service. Seeing the fortunate Gadadhara, the Lord placed His lotus feet on his head.” (CB, Antya 5.92–94)

By the Lord's wish Purandara Pandita, Parameshvari Dasa, Raghunatha Vaidya and others came there as well (CB, Antya 5.95–109).12

Later, when Raghunatha Dasa, at Nityananda's command, held the festival of flat rice with yogurt (chida-dadhi) at Panihati, Gadadhara Dasa sat with the other associates on the platform around Nityananda:

“Ramadasa, Sundarananda, Gadadhara Dasa, Murari, Kamalakara, Sadashiva, Purandara.” (CC, Antya 6.61)

According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (8.156–158), Nityananda came to Panihati with Ramadasa and Gadadhara Dasa.

After the Lord's Disappearance: Navadvipa and Katwa

According to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” Gadadhara Dasa lived in Navadvipa and took care of Shachimata and Vishnupriya Devi, managing their affairs. When they left this world, he settled in Katwa — the place of the Lord's sannyasa from Keshava Bharati — and installed a Deity of Gauranga. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya”: “In Katwa he had the service of Gaura.” This temple is known in Katwa as the “house of Mahaprabhu” (mahaprabhu-bari); according to one of the biographies, his samadhi is now there, beside the Deity. According to the “Anubhashya,” after Mahaprabhu's departure Gadadhara Dasa left Navadvipa for Katwa (Srila Bhaktisiddhanta refers here to the “Bhakti-ratnakara,” 7), and from there came to Endiyadaha and settled there; the “Narottama-vilasa,” the “Prema-vilasa” and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” find him in Katwa in the years after Vishnupriya's departure.13

According to the “Advaita-prakasha” (22), after Shachi's departure Ishana, together with Gadadhara Dasa and Sri Rama Pandita, goes in to Vishnupriya.

After the Lord's disappearance the elder associates lived in the grief of separation, and their consolation came to be the young Srinivasa and Narottama. When Srinivasa came to Navadvipa, all received him:

“Sri Murari, Srivasa Pandita, Damodara, Sanjaya, Vijaya, Shuklambara Brahmachari, Dasa Gadadhara and the other dear ones of the Lord — all showed mercy to Srinivasa. Although in separation from the Lord all were nearly dead, yet by the Lord's will they felt joy. For the sake of mercy to Srinivasa — for this [the Lord] kept His associates manifest.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 4.57–60)

Later Srinivasa came to him at Kantakanagara (Katwa). Gadadhara Dasa embraced him, asked about the Vaishnavas of Vrindavana and the Gosvamis, rejoiced and blessed him: “You will surely taste the nectar of the Lord's sankirtana among His associates; go and marry — it will bring you good.” When Srinivasa married, Gadadhara Dasa and Narahari Sarakara rejoiced in it especially.

The “Anuragavalli” (2–3) relates that Gadadhara Pandita in Puri sent a riddle to his namesake through Srinivasa, but Srinivasa forgot to deliver it. Dasa Gadadhara, who already knew of the Pandita's departure, drove him away in grief, but at Vishnupriya's intercession forgave and blessed him. His bhava is inconceivable: now laughter, now stupor, now the madness of separation; and his breath scorched one who doubted him. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” too speaks of the love of the two Gadadharas: “What wondrous love Gadadhara Pandita has with Gadadhara Dasa — who can understand it?” (1.173); sending Srinivasa from Puri to Gauda, the Pandita lamented greatly for Gadadhara Dasa, dear to him as his life (3.281).

In Navadvipa-Mayapur Narottama met the elder associates of the Lord — Shuklambara, Ishana, Murari, Damodara and Dasa Gadadhara — grieving over His disappearance. He came to Katwa as well, to the house of Gadadhara Dasa; there he saw the Deity of Gaura whom Gadadhara served: “Gaurachandra is the life of Dasa Gadadhara,” says the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (8.453), and on seeing Him Narottama could not restrain his feelings. Narottama prostrated himself before Gadadhara Dasa, who embraced him lovingly and bathed him with tears. Gadadhara Dasa passed his days aching in separation from Gaura and Nityananda; Narottama stayed with him two days.

According to the “Narottama-vilasa” (5), it was Yadunandana Chakravarti who brought Narottama to Dasa Gadadhara, who after Vishnupriya's departure was living in Katwa in grief, and Gadadhara Dasa foretold that the Lord would dance in Narottama's kirtana.

His disciple was Yadunandana Chakravarti of Katwa: the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls him “the learned Yadunandana Chakravarti, whose guru and worshipful lord was Gadadhara Dasa” (9.332).14 Shyamananda too, returning from Kheturi, stayed with Gadadhara Dasa at Kantakanagara.

His grief in these years is not worldly sorrow but the separation of an eternal associate from the Lord — the very vipralambha in which Mahaprabhu and His intimates lived.

Departure and Samadhi

According to our calendar the day of Gadadhara Dasa's departure from this world is observed on Goshthashtami (Gopashtami) — the shukla-ashtami (Gaura-ashtami) of the month of Damodara, on the same day as Srinivasa Acharya and Dhananjaya Pandita (in 2026, on 17 November). The year of his departure the sources do not give.15

According to the “Prema-vilasa” (19), in his grief for Vishnupriya he grew weak and disappeared; after him Narahari Sarakara also departed. Srinivasa, grieving over the departure of Shuklambara, Gadadhara Dasa, Narahari and Dvija Haridasa, went again to Vrindavana, and on his return took part in the festivals of separation: for Gadadhara Dasa in Katwa, for Narahari in Shrikhanda, for Dvija Haridasa in Kanchanagaria. The festival held by Srinivasa on the day of Gadadhara Dasa's departure was immense and became as renowned as the festival at Kheturi (“Bhakti-ratnakara,” 9). According to the “Prema-vilasa,” the memorial festival in Katwa was arranged by Yadunandana Chakravarti and Raghunandana, and the branches of Mahaprabhu, Nityananda, Advaita and Gadadhara gathered for it.16

Later, when Jahnava came to Katwa with her companions, all beheld “the Gauranga of Dasa Gadadhara” and the place where the Lord took sannyasa; and Yadunandana, remembering his beloved Dasa Gadadhara, could not be calm for a long while (“Narottama-vilasa” 6.274, 6.289).

The biographies mention “the festival of Gadadhara Dasa in Katwa,” attended by Raghunandana and Kamalakara Pippalai; to all appearances it is the same memorial festival.17

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that when Gadadhara Dasa departed, his samadhi was made at Endiyadaha. The biographies also speak of a samadhi in Katwa, in the “house of Mahaprabhu,” beside the samadhi of Keshava Bharati.18

Of the shripat at Ariadaha Srila Bhaktisiddhanta tells further. The samadhi there had been in the keeping of samyogi Vaishnavas; at the instruction of the siddha Srila Bhagavan Dasa Babaji of Kalna, Madhusudana Mallik of Narikeldanga in Calcutta founded a temple estate (patbari) there and began the service of the Deity of Sri Radhakanta (in the Bengali year 1256, about 1849–1850). His son Balai Mallik in 1312 (about 1905–1906) established the service of Sri Gaura-Nitai. On the altar are the Deities of Gaura-Nityananda and Radha-Krishna, and beneath it a Sanskrit verse is carved; there too is the Shiva-linga of Gopeshvara. All this is recorded on a stone at the entrance.19

The Two Gadadharas

In the Bengali year 1340 (about 1933) a booklet appeared, “Dasa Gadadhara-tattva.” Its author, posing as a zealous admirer of Dasa Gadadhara, set Gadadhara Pandita against him in a sectarian spirit: supposedly the Pandita, having studied nyaya, was at first unwilling to follow Dasa Gadadhara, the expounder of the “Bhagavatam,” but later, seeing that he lacked the taste of Gauranga's pastimes, became a disciple of Pundarika Vidyanidhi and adopted the mood of Dasa Gadadhara; and so the Pandita's followers had better leave him and follow the Dasa. Such a view is the height of godlessness (pashandita).

The two Gadadharas must not be divided and set against each other: both are associates of Gaura, His own people, eternal associates in both Gaura-lila and Vraja-lila. To honour one and disregard the other is what the “Charitamrita” calls the logic of half a hen:

“You have faith in one but show the other no respect: your standard is the logic of half a hen.” (CC, Adi 5.176)

The acharyas taught no such logic. The difference of which Karnapura and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta speak (Radha Herself and the radiance of Her body) is no ground for rivalry, but different services within one lila.

In Other Original Sources

Lochana Dasa, in the Sutra-khanda of the “Chaitanya-mangala,” names him among the associates who descended with the Lord. Jayananda in his “Chaitanya-mangala,” listing the wonders of Nityananda's associates, tells that Gadadhara Dasa threw himself into fire — as Vrindavana Dasa too says, fire, snakes and wild beasts cannot harm those who have love for Krishna (CB, Antya 5.417). And Vrindavana Dasa at once adds: by His mercy Nityananda bestowed on all His dear associates the bhavas Brahma longs for — the anuraga manifest in the gopis (CB, Antya 5.418–419); Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” calls their Krishna-bhava genuine, not artificial. Devakinandana in the “Vaishnava-vandana” ascribes to Gadadhara Dasa the wonder of a karavi bud that became fragrant like a lotus;20 he also glorifies him as “Radhika,” “the daughter of Vrishabhanu.”21

Narahari Chakravarti, too, prays to him in the “Namamrita-samudra,” his book of appeals to the Lord's associates:

“Gadadhara Dasa, keep me at those feet, that in life and in death I may never forget Gauranga.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 16)

Significance

Vrindavana Dasa, concluding the story of the Kazi, says: “Such is the glory of Gadadhara Dasa, who is counted among the associates of Lord Chaitanya” (CB, Antya 5.413); and elsewhere:

“Gadadhara Dasa was full of the rasas of divine love; merely by seeing him people were freed from all sins.” (CB, Antya 5.727)

Gadadhara Dasa is Chandrakanti, the radiance of Radha and the radiance of Gaura Himself; Purnananda too abided in him, and Nityananda acted in him. Therefore he belongs to both Gaura and Nityananda: in the Avadhuta's circle he carried the madhura-rasa of Vraja.

His life shows that the mood of a gopi is a matter of the heart, not of dress: genuine bhava springs from one's eternal spiritual form and needs no outward imitation, while dressing up the body is a distortion that no follower of Srila Rupa ever approved. His fearlessness before the Kazi teaches that only one empowered by Krishna can spread the name of Hari, and that the mercy of a great soul can touch even one whom no one dares approach. And as the Lord delivered Chand Kazi, so His servant delivered the Kazi of his own village: the servant follows in the footsteps of the Lord. Lastly, one must never speak of him so as to belittle the other Gadadhara: both are eternal associates of Gaura.

Notes

  1. Gadadhara Pandita is Radha Herself (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 147–153). Nor should he be confused with Gadadhara Dasa Dvivedi, author of the “Sampradaya-pradipa,” a disciple of Vitthalanatha of the Vallabha tradition. The “Gadadhara” in Vrindavana Dasa's lists of the Lord's associates (in the Madhya-khanda) is usually Gadadhara Pandita. One of the biographies headed a chapter on Gadadhara Pandita with his name but devoted almost all of it to Gadadhara Dasa.
  2. The biographies say eight miles north of Calcutta (one of them, 8–10 miles).
  3. One of the biographies ascribes the words about “the beauty of the body of Vrishabhanu's daughter” to the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” itself (and cites it with a misprint: “154-54” for 154–155). Karnapura says only “a manifestation of Radha's glory” (radha-vibhuti-rupa); “the beauty of the body” and “radiance” are Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's words.
  4. This passage is found only in the 1983 edition of the “Chaitanya-mangala.”
  5. The Bengali verse says simply “Gadadhara” (gadadhara); the earlier Russian translation had “Gadadhara Dasa” here, which has been corrected in the revised one. Whom exactly the verse means, the sources do not specify.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta mentions the pot separately: “sometimes” Gadadhara in the bhava of a gopi bore on his head a full pot of Ganga water and sold it as milk. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” on the way he only cried “Who will buy yogurt?” (Antya 5.238), while the pot of Ganga water and the cry “Who will buy milk?” come later, in his house, when Nityananda arrived (Antya 5.372–373).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that Madhava Ghosha, with the help of Nityananda and Dasa Gadadhara, sang and danced before the Deity of Gopala, enacting (abhinaya) the “Dana-khanda.” The biographies tell it differently: according to one, Nityananda watched the dana-lila as revealed by Madhavananda Ghosha and fell into trance; according to another, following the “Chaitanya-bhagavata,” Madhavananda sang and Nityananda danced. In every case this is no worldly show but a lila of Krishna revealed in Nityananda's kirtana and dance.
  10. One of the biographies adds that Gadadhara lovingly embraced the Kazi, and that the Kazi had come out to punish the disturber of the peace but, seeing Gadadhara's form, the embodiment of Radhika's radiance, was astonished; another, that the Kazi, seeing him in trance, calmed down.
  11. One of the biographies adds that the Kazi, purified by the mercy of Gadadhara and of the Name, took shelter at his feet, and that thus Gadadhara Dasa delivered countless sinners, unbelievers and yavanas. In the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” the Kazi only promises to chant the Name tomorrow — and in doing so already utters it.
  12. In the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Antya 5) the Lord's journey through Gauda is described before He sends Nityananda to Gauda; according to the “Charitamrita,” Nityananda was sent earlier (Madhya 15.42–44), and the Lord's journey through Gauda towards Vrindavana came later (Madhya 16). We follow the “Charitamrita.” One of the biographies calls the meeting at Panihati Gadadhara Dasa's first meeting with Mahaprabhu; but according to the “Charitamrita” he was already a devotee of Sri Chaitanya (Adi 11.13), Vrindavana Dasa calls him “infinitely dear to the Lord,” and the padas and Lochana Dasa show him beside the Lord in Navadvipa and Shantipur.

According to one of the biographies, his shripat was at Ariadaha, and after Mahaprabhu's disappearance he moved to Katwa; the others follow the “Anubhashya.” According to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” he settled in Katwa after the departure of Shachi and Vishnupriya; the “Narottama-vilasa,” the “Prema-vilasa” and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” find him in Katwa (Kantakanagara) in his last years too. Where he left this world, the sources do not say outright.

  16. According to one of the biographies, he departed later — after Srinivasa's second visit to Vrindavana: returning to Yajigrama, Srinivasa learned at Kantakanagara that Gadadhara Dasa had departed in Kartika.

  21. According to the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (154) he is Chandrakanti, a manifestation of Radha's glory, and according to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta the radiance, the beauty of Radha's body; Radha Herself is Gadadhara Pandita. So these words of the “Vaishnava-vandana” are to be understood.
